summary: Summarizes the impact Multipath TCP may have on applications. Although it is designed to be backward compatible, its data transport differs from regular TCP and gives applications extra options to exploit. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Using several roads to deliver one package works like normal delivery, but the sender has extra choices. This tells app builders what they might want to know.

questions: does mptcp work with existing applications
subtitle: What Multipath TCP means for applications, and the small set of socket options for apps that want to control it.

tldr.problem: Multipath TCP is designed to be invisible to applications, but one connection can now span several subflows and addresses, which changes performance and breaks some assumptions that applications make.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes the performance and compatibility effects on legacy applications, then defines a basic abstract sockets API of five MPTCP options for applications that are MPTCP-aware.
tldr.outcome: It is informational guidance for application and stack developers; an advanced API is explicitly left out of scope.

today: RFC 6897 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. Its API is an abstract basic API, and the RFC leaves an advanced API for further study.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
Multipath TCP (MPTCP) adds the ability to use multiple paths to a regular TCP session. It offers the same reliable, in-order byte stream as TCP and is designed to be backward compatible with applications and the network. Both endpoints need MPTCP support in their network stacks.

The RFC does three things: it presents the effects MPTCP may have on applications, defines how MPTCP interoperates with applications that are unaware of it, and specifies a basic API for MPTCP-aware applications. The basic API is an abstract extension of the sockets interface giving the equivalent control and information that regular TCP offers. An advanced API with finer-grained control over path management and scheduling is out of scope, though the appendix lists possible features.
sections.plainLanguage: A normal delivery uses one road. This kind uses several roads at once, and the paper explains what that means for the programs that send and receive.

sections.title: Effects on Performance and Possible Problems
sections.content:
MPTCP aims to do at least as well as single-path TCP. Throughput usually improves because several paths are pooled, and can exceed the capacity of a single interface, but it may vary more as subflows come and go, which matters to streaming applications. MPTCP signaling adds a small overhead. Delay and jitter can get worse when subflow delays differ, because data is spread across them, though in-order delivery to the application is still guaranteed. Jitter-sensitive applications can disable MPTCP. Resilience improves because traffic can move to the remaining subflows if one fails, and a connection can survive an address change.

On the problem side, some middleboxes may block or strip the TCP options MPTCP uses; MPTCP then falls back to regular TCP, possibly after extra setup delay, and a Happy Eyeballs style parallel attempt is suggested. Applications that need a single path, such as bandwidth measurement tools or BGP, can disable MPTCP. An MPTCP-unaware application that logs addresses will see only the first subflow.
sections.plainLanguage: More roads usually means a faster, safer trip, and if one road closes the trip goes on. But packages can arrive in more uneven bursts, and a few programs that expect exactly one road will be confused.

sections.title: Legacy Applications and Socket Behavior
sections.content:
Legacy applications use the standard sockets API unchanged, which is the default case. MPTCP sits between the sockets interface and the TCP subflows. The mapping between a socket and a flow is now one to many, so some calls need care.

  • Binding: if an application binds to a specific address or interface, MPTCP MUST respect that, which disables MPTCP for the connection unless multipath-aware calls are used. Binding to INADDR_ANY lets local policy set up multiple subflows.
  • Addresses: for legacy applications getpeername() and getsockname() MUST return the addresses and ports of the first subflow, even if it is no longer in use. A stack MAY close the whole connection when the first subflow closes (fate-sharing), at the cost of reduced resilience.
  • close(): semantics are unchanged; MPTCP closes the connection with Data FIN.
  • Socket options: existing options SHOULD apply to all subflows. TCP_NODELAY SHOULD disable the Nagle algorithm on every subflow. Very small send or receive buffers make MPTCP inefficient, so an implementation MAY treat them as a request not to use MPTCP. Urgent data is not recommended with MPTCP.

Whether MPTCP is enabled by default is local policy. Even when enabled, it is used only if both endpoints support it and at least one has multiple addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Old programs keep working because MPTCP quietly tells them about the first road only. If a program says exactly which road to use, MPTCP does not argue.

sections.title: The Basic API for MPTCP-Aware Applications
sections.content:
The basic API is based on four core requirements: an application should be able to turn MPTCP on or off (REQ1), restrict MPTCP to a given set of addresses (REQ2), get the pairs of addresses used by subflows (REQ3), and extract a unique connection identifier (REQ4). It is described abstractly as new values on a socket, which could be implemented through setsockopt() and getsockopt() or as new function calls.

  • TCP_MULTIPATH_ENABLE is set before connection setup and read afterward. Setting it to true means the stack SHOULD try to negotiate MPTCP, although MPTCP still needs support at both ends and a usable path. Setting it to false means MPTCP MUST NOT be used.
  • TCP_MULTIPATH_ADD binds MPTCP to a list of local addresses, or adds addresses during a connection. A port number may be given. The addresses are only a hint to the peer, and the implementation MAY use a subset.
  • TCP_MULTIPATH_REMOVE removes local addresses; MPTCP MUST close the matching subflows and signal the removal to the peer.
  • TCP_MULTIPATH_SUBFLOWS is read-only and returns the pairs of local and remote address and port of established subflows.
  • TCP_MULTIPATH_CONNID is read-only and returns a locally unique connection identifier, which SHOULD be an integer such as the MPTCP token.
sections.plainLanguage: A program that knows about the many roads gets a few switches: use roads or not, which roads to use, a list of the roads in use, and a ticket number for the trip.

sections.title: Other Compatibility Issues and Security
sections.content:
When TLS compares addresses with names in X.509 certificates, it MUST only use the address of the initial subflow. MPTCP can conflict with other multihoming APIs, so multiaddressed MPTCP SHOULD NOT be enabled if the stack uses SHIM6, HIP or Mobile IPv6. MPTCP MUST NOT assume that several A or AAAA records from one DNS query refer to the same host.

On security, the RFC notes that applications which signal addresses or make security decisions based on address queries, for example opening firewall holes, may need MPTCP disabled by administrators. Applications should use TCP_MULTIPATH_ADD with care, since new subflows may be established and the addresses may be advertised to the peer, which could leak the addresses of otherwise invisible interfaces. Using different addresses should not be assumed to mean using different paths.
sections.plainLanguage: Telling the other side about all your roads can give away more than you meant to, so a program should only list the roads it is happy to share.
